screens.title: Searching Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore why searching is central to efficient software. You already know linear search: check each element until you find the target. That works for small or unsorted data, but it becomes impractical as data grows. Here we introduce binary search, a divide-and-conquer approach that requires sorted input and reduces comparisons from proportional to the list size down to proportional to its logarithm. We'll trace binary search step by step with a concrete sorted array and show both iterative and recursive implementations in C. Finally, we'll introduce the idea of hashing — a different strategy that can give average-case constant-time lookups with a hash table and a good hash function. You will learn when to choose sorting plus binary search and when hashing might be a better fit. To ground this, think of looking up a name in a million-entry phone book versus computing a hash to jump straight to a bucket. By the end, you'll understand the trade-offs: when sorting cost makes binary search unattractive, and how collisions affect hashing. Consider which approach fits your data and operations as we proceed.

Searching Algorithms

Understand how algorithm choice changes performance. We'll contrast linear and binary search, step through C implementations, and introduce hashing so you can decide which lookup strategy fits your data.

In this lesson

Choosing the right search approach can turn an infeasible operation on large datasets into something fast and practical.

Linear vs Binary
Linear checks elements one-by-one. Binary halves the search space but needs sorted data.
Binary Search
Divide and conquer yields O(log n) comparisons for sorted arrays.
Hashing

Binary Search Mechanics
Low, high, mid and repeated halving for sorted arrays.

Iterative and recursive patterns with careful mid calculation.

Hash functions, tables, and simple collision strategies.

These practical skills let you choose and implement a search strategy that fits the data you have and the operations you need.

screens.title: Linear Search: straightforward but slow at scale
screens.narratorSegment: Linear search inspects each element in sequence until it finds the target or reaches the end. That definition is simple, and the simplicity is its strength for small or unsorted collections. But the cost grows linearly with the number of items: on average and in the worst case it is O(n). Practically, that means a list of a million items could require a million checks to find an element or confirm it isn't present. A common real-world example is scanning an unsorted list of names one by one. The explanation is straightforward: no structure guides the search. Important misconceptions include thinking that a clever pointer or an early exit will change average complexity; it doesn't change the asymptotic cost for arbitrary inputs. When you need many repeated lookups, or your dataset is already sorted, linear search is rarely the right choice. Use linear search when lists are tiny, when the list is unsorted and you will only search once, or when simplicity trumps performance. Key takeaway: linear search is easy to write and reason about, but it does not scale well.

screens.title: Binary Search: definition and prerequisite
screens.narratorSegment: Binary search is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that finds an element in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search interval. The crucial prerequisite is that the array must be sorted. Without sorting, comparisons do not provide guaranteed information about where the target might be, and binary search will fail. The algorithm tracks two indices: low and high. It computes mid as low plus half the distance to high, compares the element at mid to the target, and then discards the half that cannot contain the target. This repeat-until-empty pattern yields logarithmic growth in comparisons. A helpful safety note, especially in C, is to compute mid as low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2 to avoid potential integer overflow on extreme indexes. A common misconception is believing binary search can be applied directly to unsorted data; it cannot. Another subtle error arises when updating low and high incorrectly leading to missed elements or infinite loops. Remember: sorted data and careful boundary updates are what make binary search correct and efficient. Binary Search: definition and prerequisite means binary search requires a sorted array and careful index updates; use mid = low + (high - low)/2 to avoid overflow.. In practical terms, divide and conquer applied to sorted arrays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 3.3 › Binary Search
Formal definition
A search that halves the candidate interval on each comparison, requiring a sorted array to guarantee correctness.
Key indices
  • low — start index of current interval
  • high — end index of current interval
  • mid — low + (high - low) / 2, used to compare with target
Common-mistake
Applying binary search to unsorted arrays or miscalculating mid can cause incorrect results or infinite loops.
Concrete example
Sorted array requirement: if numbers are not ordered, a mid comparison gives no reliable direction. Sorting first can cost O(n log n), so weigh that cost against repeated queries.
Why it matters
With sorted data, binary search turns a potentially expensive lookup into a fast one, dramatically improving performance for repeated queries.
Check your understanding
If your dataset is unsorted but you only need one lookup, is sorting first always worth it? Consider the total cost of sorting plus search versus a single linear scan.

screens.title: Binary Search Steps — halving the interval
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk in detail through a single binary search process. Start with low set to the first index and high set to the last index. While low is less than or equal to high, compute mid as low plus half the distance to high to avoid overflow. Compare arr[mid] to the target. If equal, return mid — we're done. If arr[mid] is less than the target, the target must live in the right half, so update low to mid plus one. If arr[mid] is greater than the target, update high to mid minus one to keep the left half. The loop invariant is that the target, if present, lies between low and high inclusive. Repeat until low exceeds high; at that point the target is not in the array. A common pitfall is off-by-one when updating low or high; always use mid + 1 and mid - 1 respectively. This ensures progress and that the invariant holds. Tracing concrete indices on a sample array helps make the invariant tangible and prevents logical errors. In practical terms, concrete step-by-step algorithm with loop invariants. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 3.3 › Binary Search Steps
Step-by-step
  1. Set low = 0 and high = size - 1.
  2. While low <= high: compute mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
  3. Compare arr[mid] to target: if equal, return mid.
  4. If arr[mid] < target, set low = mid + 1; else set high = mid - 1.
  5. If loop ends, target not found; return -1.
Invariant and progress
Invariant: if the target exists it is in [low,high]. Each update reduces interval size, so the loop must terminate.
Concrete trace
Given [2,5,8,12,16,23,38,56,72,91] searching for 23: initial low 0, high 9, mid 4 gives 16 < 23 so low becomes 5; next mid 7 gives 56 > 23 so high becomes 6; next mid 5 equals 23 and returns index 5.
Common mistake
Using mid = (low + high) / 2 can overflow for extreme indexes in some languages; prefer low + (high - low) / 2.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 3.3 › Iterative Binary Search
Code (iterative)
#include <stdio.h>

// Function to perform iterative binary search
int binary_search_iterative(int arr[], int size, int target) {
  int low = 0;
  int high = size - 1;

  while (low <= high) {
    int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; // Prevent potential overflow

    if (arr[mid] == target) {
      return mid;
    }

    if (arr[mid] < target) {
      low = mid + 1;
    } else {
      high = mid - 1;
    }
  }

  return -1; // Target not found
}
Testing notes
Always test with targets at the start, middle, end, and absent values. These cases reveal off-by-one errors and improper loop conditions.
Concrete example
Using the provided sorted array, searching for 23 returns index 5; searching for 100 returns -1.
Key Takeaway

Compute mid safely and update low/high with mid+1 or mid-1. Test both hits and misses.

Module 1 › Chapter 3.3 › Recursive Binary Search
Starter code
#include <stdio.h>

int binary_search_recursive(int arr[], int low, int high, int target) {
  // Base case: empty interval
  if (low > high) {
    return -1;
  }

  int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;

  if (arr[mid] == target) {
    return mid;
  }

  if (arr[mid] < target) {
    return binary_search_recursive(arr, mid + 1, high, target);
  } else {
    return binary_search_recursive(arr, low, mid - 1, target);
  }
}
Activity
Implement the recursive function and run it on the sample array to verify index results for present and absent targets. Compare outputs with the iterative version.
Pro tip
Trace one recursive call by hand to ensure your low and high updates match the iterative logic and to verify the base case fires correctly.
Key Takeaway

Recursion expresses halving compactly, but you must ensure correct base case and index updates to avoid stack issues or missed elements.

Now low is five, high is nine; mid becomes seven and arr[mid] is 56. Because 56 is greater than 23, set high to six. Now low is five, high is six; mid becomes five and arr[mid] is 23, a match, so return five. This three-step trace shows how the search space is halved and how each comparison eliminates the impossible half. Also trace a miss: searching for a value not present reduces the interval until low exceeds high and returns -1. screens.title: Time Complexity: O(log n) explained

If you start with n elements, after one comparison you have at most n/2 candidates, then n/4, then n/8, and so on. The number of halvings needed until one element remains is logarithmic in n, specifically on the order of log base two of n. Practically, this is extremely efficient: for one million elements, binary search requires about twenty comparisons in the worst case. Contrast that with linear search which may require up to one million comparisons. Best-case cost for binary search is constant time when the target is found at the first mid. screens.title: Off-by-one errors and mid calculation pitfalls

screens.title: Hashing basics
screens.narratorSegment: Hashing is a technique to map arbitrary keys to indices in an array called a hash table using a hash function. The hash function takes a key and returns a numeric index within the table bounds. When the function distributes keys uniformly, lookups, insertions, and deletions can be done in average-case constant time, O(1). This is powerful when you need many dynamic operations because you avoid sorting and repeated halving. However, collisions are inevitable: different keys may map to the same index. Handling collisions is essential, and that is where design choices matter. Two common approaches are separate chaining, where each bucket holds a linked list of entries, and open addressing, where the algorithm probes for the next available slot. A simple example hash function is key modulo table size, which is easy to compute but can cluster values if keys share a pattern. Hashing trades deterministic worst-case guarantees for very fast average performance with good function design and maintenance of table load factors. screens.title: Collision resolution strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Collisions are inevitable in a finite hash table, so resolution strategies determine performance in practice. Separate chaining stores a linked list (or other container) at each table index; when multiple keys hash to the same bucket, append them there. Lookup checks the bucket and searches the small list. If the hash distributes keys evenly, these lists remain short and operations stay near O(1) on average. Open addressing keeps all entries in the table itself and resolves collisions by probing for another slot, for example by checking the next slot, or using quadratic probing. Each approach has trade-offs: separate chaining simplifies growth and can handle higher load factors, but requires secondary memory for lists. Open addressing keeps memory compact but performance degrades as the table fills and requires careful probing strategies. In either case, choosing table size, managing load factor, and selecting a good hash function are critical to achieving fast average performance. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore why searching is central to efficient software. You already know linear search: check each element until you find the target. That works for small or unsorted data, but it becomes impractical as data grows. Here we introduce binary search, a divide-and-conquer approach that requires sorted input and reduces comparisons from proportional to the list size down to proportional to its logarithm. We'll trace binary search step by step with a concrete sorted array and show both iterative and recursive implementations in C. Finally, we'll introduce the idea of hashing — a different strategy that can give average-case constant-time lookups with a hash table and a good hash function. You will learn when to choose sorting plus binary search and when hashing might be a better fit. To ground this, think of looking up a name in a million-entry phone book versus computing a hash to jump straight to a bucket. By the end, you'll understand the trade-offs: when sorting cost makes binary search unattractive, and how collisions affect hashing. Consider which approach fits your data and operations as we proceed.

In this first set of objectives we make explicit the skills you'll develop. First, you'll recall the limits of linear search: it inspects each element and is O(n) on average and in the worst case, which is impractical for very large lists. Second, you'll learn the prerequisites for using binary search — most importantly that the data must be sorted — and why sorting first can change the overall cost. Third, you will implement the iterative form of binary search in C, practicing careful index arithmetic and an overflow-safe mid calculation. Fourth, you'll begin to reason about why halving the search space leads to logarithmic time. Each objective connects concept, practice, and reason: recognizing when linear search is insufficient, understanding why order matters for binary search, writing safe index code in C, and forming the intuition behind O(log n). These practical skills let you choose and implement a search strategy that fits the data you have and the operations you need.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and extension. First, you'll implement recursive binary search in C, learning to express the halving step as a recursive call and to stop at clear base cases. Second, you'll analyze time complexity formally: best, average, and worst cases for binary search and how those compare to linear search. Third, you'll be introduced to hashing: what a hash function and hash table are, and why hashing can yield average-case constant time for lookup. Fourth, you'll learn about collisions and simple resolution strategies like separate chaining and open addressing, so you understand the trade-offs and when hashing might degrade to linear time. Together these objectives move you from understanding the algorithm to implementing, analyzing, and choosing among strategies for real datasets. Learning Objectives — Practice & Extension means practice recursive implementation, analyze complexity, and learn hashing fundamentals and collision handling.. In practical terms, applying and verifying binary search and hashing knowledge. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Linear search inspects each element in sequence until it finds the target or reaches the end. That definition is simple, and the simplicity is its strength for small or unsorted collections. But the cost grows linearly with the number of items: on average and in the worst case it is O(n). Practically, that means a list of a million items could require a million checks to find an element or confirm it isn't present. A common real-world example is scanning an unsorted list of names one by one. The explanation is straightforward: no structure guides the search. Important misconceptions include thinking that a clever pointer or an early exit will change average complexity; it doesn't change the asymptotic cost for arbitrary inputs. When you need many repeated lookups, or your dataset is already sorted, linear search is rarely the right choice. Use linear search when lists are tiny, when the list is unsorted and you will only search once, or when simplicity trumps performance. Key takeaway: linear search is easy to write and reason about, but it does not scale well.

Binary search is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that finds an element in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search interval. The crucial prerequisite is that the array must be sorted. Without sorting, comparisons do not provide guaranteed information about where the target might be, and binary search will fail. The algorithm tracks two indices: low and high. It computes mid as low plus half the distance to high, compares the element at mid to the target, and then discards the half that cannot contain the target. This repeat-until-empty pattern yields logarithmic growth in comparisons. A helpful safety note, especially in C, is to compute mid as low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2 to avoid potential integer overflow on extreme indexes. A common misconception is believing binary search can be applied directly to unsorted data; it cannot. Another subtle error arises when updating low and high incorrectly leading to missed elements or infinite loops. Remember: sorted data and careful boundary updates are what make binary search correct and efficient. Binary Search: definition and prerequisite means binary search requires a sorted array and careful index updates; use mid = low + (high - low)/2 to avoid overflow.. In practical terms, divide and conquer applied to sorted arrays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk in detail through a single binary search process. Start with low set to the first index and high set to the last index. While low is less than or equal to high, compute mid as low plus half the distance to high to avoid overflow. Compare arr[mid] to the target. If equal, return mid — we're done. If arr[mid] is less than the target, the target must live in the right half, so update low to mid plus one. If arr[mid] is greater than the target, update high to mid minus one to keep the left half. The loop invariant is that the target, if present, lies between low and high inclusive. Repeat until low exceeds high; at that point the target is not in the array. A common pitfall is off-by-one when updating low or high; always use mid + 1 and mid - 1 respectively. This ensures progress and that the invariant holds. Tracing concrete indices on a sample array helps make the invariant tangible and prevents logical errors. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we'll look at the iterative C implementation and explain why each line matters. The function initializes low to zero and high to size minus one. The while loop runs while low is less than or equal to high. Each iteration computes mid as low plus the half distance to high to prevent overflow, then compares arr[mid] to target. If equal, return mid. If arr[mid] is less than the target, set low to mid plus one; otherwise set high to mid minus one. If the loop completes without finding the target, return negative one to signal absence. In the main function we show two searches: one that succeeds and one that fails. Notice the print logic differentiates these outcomes. A practical tip: always test both hit and miss cases and choose sample arrays that exercise leftmost and rightmost elements to detect off-by-one bugs. This iterative pattern avoids recursion overhead and is straightforward when you track low and high carefully. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Recursive binary search expresses the halving logic as a function that calls itself on a smaller interval. The base case is when low exceeds high: return negative one to signal absence. Otherwise compute mid and compare arr[mid] to the target. If equal, return mid. If arr[mid] is less, recursively search the right half by calling the function with mid plus one and high. If arr[mid] is greater, recursively search the left half with low and mid minus one. The starter code in the chapter already shows correct recursive calls for both halves; your task is to ensure the base case and the correct indices are used. Recursion makes the logic succinct but introduces call stack considerations and potential overhead. Binary search requires at most logarithmic comparisons because each comparison halves the number of possible positions for the target. If you start with n elements, after one comparison you have at most n/2 candidates, then n/4, then n/8, and so on. The number of halvings needed until one element remains is logarithmic in n, specifically on the order of log base two of n. Practically, this is extremely efficient: for one million elements, binary search requires about twenty comparisons in the worst case. Contrast that with linear search which may require up to one million comparisons. Best-case cost for binary search is constant time when the target is found at the first mid. Average and worst cases are both O(log n). An important nuance: sorting a dataset first costs time—often O(n log n)—so the full workflow matters. If you must sort once and then perform many searches, binary search often wins. If you have only one search and the data is unsorted, a single linear scan might be cheaper overall. A frequent source of bugs in binary search is off-by-one errors or an unsafe mid calculation. Using mid = (low + high) / 2 in languages with fixed-size integers can overflow when low and high are large. The safer formula mid = low + (high - low) / 2 avoids summing two large numbers. Another pitfall is updating low and high incorrectly. After comparing arr[mid] and target, you must set low to mid + 1 when discarding the left half or set high to mid - 1 when discarding the right half. Failing to add or subtract one can leave mid unchanged and cause infinite loops, or skip possible positions and miss the target. Hashing is a technique to map arbitrary keys to indices in an array called a hash table using a hash function. The hash function takes a key and returns a numeric index within the table bounds. When the function distributes keys uniformly, lookups, insertions, and deletions can be done in average-case constant time, O(1). This is powerful when you need many dynamic operations because you avoid sorting and repeated halving. However, collisions are inevitable: different keys may map to the same index. Handling collisions is essential, and that is where design choices matter. Two common approaches are separate chaining, where each bucket holds a linked list of entries, and open addressing, where the algorithm probes for the next available slot. A simple example hash function is key modulo table size, which is easy to compute but can cluster values if keys share a pattern. Hashing trades deterministic worst-case guarantees for very fast average performance with good function design and maintenance of table load factors. Collisions are inevitable in a finite hash table, so resolution strategies determine performance in practice. Separate chaining stores a linked list (or other container) at each table index; when multiple keys hash to the same bucket, append them there. Lookup checks the bucket and searches the small list. If the hash distributes keys evenly, these lists remain short and operations stay near O(1) on average. Open addressing keeps all entries in the table itself and resolves collisions by probing for another slot, for example by checking the next slot, or using quadratic probing. Each approach has trade-offs: separate chaining simplifies growth and can handle higher load factors, but requires secondary memory for lists. Open addressing keeps memory compact but performance degrades as the table fills and requires careful probing strategies. In either case, choosing table size, managing load factor, and selecting a good hash function are critical to achieving fast average performance.
